Your manager needs more repeat customers. Your customers need to understand what they are choosing.</p><div class="callout"><strong>How to play</strong><p>Read each scene and choose an action. There is no timer or score. Different choices reveal different consequences. Sound is optional; use the control above.</p></div><div class="credits-mini"><strong>Team 24 · CMPT 376W G1</strong><p>Edward Lu — <em>role to confirm</em><br>Oak Soe Khant — <em>role to confirm</em><br>Wonchan Kim — <em>role to confirm</em></p><p>Based on ACM’s <a href="https://ethics.acm.org/code-of-ethics/using-the-code/case-dark-ux-patterns/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Dark UX Patterns</a> case study. All characters, company events, prices, and legal proceedings in this story are fictional.</p></div><div class="choices"> [[Begin the story->Graduation]] [[Media and project credits->Credits]] </div></div></div><div class="passage-shell" data-scene="graduation" data-typing="false"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="A graduation cap and diploma."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/photo-of-person-holding-graduation-cap-and-diploma-7944064/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">01 / A PLACE TO START</p><h1>The offer</h1><p>You have recently graduated and have been applying for jobs for several months.</p><p>Amaze offers you a junior developer position. You accept because you need a steady income and want work experience.</p><p>On your first morning, Morgan, your software-development manager, walks you through the office.</p><blockquote>“We move quickly here. Show us you can deliver, and there’s room to grow.”</blockquote><p>You need this job to pay rent, and your family is happy that you found work.</p><p>You want to do well in your new role.</p><div class="choices"> [[Meet Morgan and see your first project->FirstProject]] </div></div></div><div class="passage-shell" data-scene="office" data-typing="false"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="An empty modern office at Amaze."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/an-empty-office-5483236/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">cottonbro studio / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">02 / THE FIRST REQUEST</p><h1>A discount, already selected</h1><p>Morgan opens the checkout for a $22 pack of household supplies. A green badge offers the same pack for <strong>$18 with Sub and Save</strong>.</p><p>The subscription option is selected before the customer touches the page. The smaller text says the item will arrive every month until cancelled.</p><div class="checkout" aria-label="Fictional checkout illustration"><span class="mini-label">AMAZE · CHECKOUT PREVIEW</span><strong>Household essentials</strong><div class="price">$18 <small>with Sub and Save</small></div><div class="selected-option">☑ Monthly subscription selected</div><p>$18 each delivery · repeats every month</p><div class="fake-button">Continue</div><span class="muted">One-time purchase: $22</span></div><blockquote>“Keep the subscription selected,” Morgan says. “Repeat orders make revenue predictable. That helps protect everyone’s jobs.”</blockquote><p>You ask whether customers will realize the discount means signing up. Morgan points at the terms.</p><blockquote>“It’s written there. This is standard optimization.”</blockquote><div class="choices"> [[Accept the project without raising an objection->Implementation]] [[Question the design and discuss the customer risks->Debate]] [[Refuse to build this checkout->BadEnding1]] </div></div></div>(set: $raisedConcern to true) <div class="passage-shell" data-scene="office" data-typing="false"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="An empty modern office at Amaze."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/an-empty-office-5483236/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">cottonbro studio / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">03 / THE OBJECTION</p><h1>“It’s a choice they can change”</h1><p>You explain that a customer may see an immediate discount and overlook the monthly commitment. Choosing a delivery frequency for someone is different from asking what they need.</p><p>Morgan listens, but does not agree.</p><blockquote>“Subscriptions can help people who rely on deliveries, including customers who find shopping in person difficult. We give them convenience and a lower price.”</blockquote><p>You agree that subscriptions can be useful. You suggest letting customers choose whether to subscribe and how often they receive an item.</p><blockquote>“You’re new,” Morgan says. “Take a smaller project for now. We’ll revisit this.”</blockquote><div class="choices"> [[Take the smaller project while keeping your concern on record->SmallerProject]] [[Agree to implement Sub and Save after the discussion->Implementation]] </div></div></div><div class="passage-shell" data-scene="office" data-typing="false"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="An empty modern office at Amaze."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/an-empty-office-5483236/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">cottonbro studio / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">04 / THE PRESSURE</p><h1>The request returns</h1><p>You spend the next two weeks fixing product-page bugs. The work is useful, but Morgan repeatedly asks when you will take on Sub and Save.</p><blockquote>“We need people who take ownership,” Morgan says during your check-in. “If you won’t do it, another developer can. Or someone can use an AI tool to draft the code.”</blockquote><p>Your refusal alone will not prevent the launch. Agreeing would give you influence over implementation, but Morgan still wants the same default.</p><p>You must answer.</p><div class="choices"> [[Relent and agree to implement it->Implementation]] [[Refuse the request again->BadEnding2]] </div></div></div><div class="passage-shell" data-scene="office" data-typing="true"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="An empty modern office at Amaze."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/an-empty-office-5483236/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">cottonbro studio / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">05 / ONE MORE CHANGE</p><h1>The numbers look good</h1><p>You build the checkout. Sub and Save is selected by default and the delivery interval begins at one month.</p><p>Before release, Taylor, the product lead, arranges a short customer test. Jamie, a volunteer customer, selects Continue.</p><blockquote>“Eighteen dollars for this order. That works for me.”</blockquote><p>When Taylor asks about the next delivery, Jamie pauses.</p><blockquote>“Next delivery? I only wanted one.”</blockquote><p>You share the result with Morgan. Morgan decides to proceed, saying customers can change the settings.</p><p>After launch, recurring orders increase. Morgan praises your speed. Then comes another request.</p><blockquote>“The higher-ups want better retention. Put cancellation deeper in account settings. Make customers open each subscription separately. Keep the edit screen for quantity and frequency only.”</blockquote><p>You now have direct evidence that some customers misunderstand the commitment.</p><div class="choices"> [[Implement the harder cancellation process->HardCancellation]] [[Refuse to add cancellation barriers->BadEnding2]] </div></div></div><div class="passage-shell" data-scene="deliveries" data-typing="true"><div class="scene-hero" role="img" aria-label="A delivery van filled with cardboard parcels."></div><p class="photo-credit">Photo: <a href="https://www.pexels.com/photo/brown-cardboard-boxes-inside-the-van-6169662/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tima Miroshnichenko / Pexels</a></p><div class="story-copy"><p class="kicker">06 / THE CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE</p><h1>Easy to enter. Hard to leave.</h1><p>You move cancellation away from the edit-subscription screen. Customers can change quantity and frequency there, but must open each item individually to stop deliveries.</p><p>The monthly default remains. Morgan calls the lower cancellation rate an improvement.</p><p>Jamie receives another pack. On the account page, he changes the quantity before realizing that doing so does not stop the subscription. He opens another menu, then another.</p><blockquote>“Why can’t I just cancel this?”</blockquote><p>The company reports better retention, but Jamie has paid for an order he did not want.</p><div
